label.rationale: Black's king and bishop escort the e-pawn; the pawn can advance first or after the bishop improves.
Nf5 allows a concrete Ng3 sequence while Nh5 and Rc7 defend via different piece coordination and control of the c-file.
Nxf3 interrupts the attack. The alternatives allow g5 and forcing rook entries, and separate strategic value is uncertain.
Black can trade on d4 immediately or improve the king first. Rook activity and the king's route to d5 drive the resulting endgame.
White can use the rook on the open a-file against the doubled a-pawns or enter from the d-file. Black's king and central break matter in both lines.
Both rook and knight coordinate immediate threats against the confined king. The pawn races are inseparable from that attack in the close lines.
Rxc5 must account for Rac8 and the exchange on c8. Independently the knight on d4 and White's f4 plan survive the candidate comparison.
The identity of the piece taking b5 changes the bishop attack and risks losing a5. White's a4 lever and Black's f-pawn break also shape the choice.
Black's queenside majority advances in all leading continuations. White can push d5 or organize rook and queen counterplay.
Black's strong extra minor piece can be coordinated via Nb5 or a central king approach after Kf8. Both plans keep usable central squares.
exd5 is the concrete way to remove the bishop before castling. White's rook entry on d7 changes the ensuing strategic balance even after the piece is recovered.
White can make progress with the queenside majority or trade rooks into the favourable bishop ending. The checks alter the timing.
Nxe6+ changes the recapture and knight access immediately. Separate plans centre on the c-file and pawn breaks b4 or exd6.
Rg3 exploits the vulnerable king if the queen takes e5. White can also advance on the f-file or aim for a queen trade to preserve the edge.
Qg6 and Rd8 force mate. The leading alternatives revolve around the same mating geometry.
Bd7+ deflects the king so Qxe5 wins a rook. The close queen checks transpose into the same material sequence.
Nc3 and Rb2 must handle different queen and rook captures. White can also improve the bishop on g3 and keep the b-file contested.
Black's c5 and f4 breaks, or Nd5 and e5, are different ways to hold the centre and free the pieces. The tactical status is less clear.
Qxe4 is a concrete exchange resource after Ndf6 and Bg5. Knight outposts and an f-pawn break shape the alternative positions.
Qh4 avoids the stronger f4 tempo and preserves Rxd8+. The rook's access to the d-file and Black's central pawn chain matter beyond the exchange.
fxe3 removes the knight attack; Nxe5 runs into Nxd1. After the removal White's queenside pawn advance targets the castled king.
White's central king routes and f4 or d4 breaks determine who gets the better pawn ending. No distinct forcing win was settled in review.
Both hxg threats and forcing rook checks are needed to handle d7. The advanced d-pawn also constrains Black's play in slower lines.
Qh5 and the liquidation on f1 arise from different capture sequences. White's connected advanced central pawns remain a separate force.
Nxe7+ and Nxg6+ win the queen in the sharpest line. a6 is an independent option for opening a queenside attack.
Black's central majority and strong c4 knight constrain White while each queen move changes the rook's route. There are forcing exchanges, with unresolved tactical dominance.
Rxe2+ gains a tempo before the a-pawn advance. Promotion pressure and White's ability to blockade on a1 are also important across choices.
Rc4 and Rc2 exploit the bishop's limited defence while denying Rxa2. The passed a-pawn dictates the alternative choices after the initial threat.
Nd5 and doubling rooks can transpose. The positional test is whether the f4 break and d-file pressure remain available after different replies.
h5 enables Bxh3 after g5. Re8 and the queen trade supply an independent plan to contest the files and manage the passed pawns.
Nxe4 changes the immediate queen and knight tactics. White can also manage the kingside pawn storm through different queen retreats and f3.
b6 exposes the queen to an attack and tactically secures liquidation through Rad1. The advanced b-pawn and resulting passed pawn are independently important.
Nxb7 wins the bishop outright and preserves the knight after Nbc5. The near-term tactical loss distinguishes the alternatives.
Qa8 allows Nxe5 and a sharp response on c5. Choosing the queen trade with Qf4 leaves an enduring central-pawn structure and a different rook ending.
Rxc3 is a concrete exchange offer with a check on b6. The h-pawn break and use of the g-file are a separate plan for White.
